title: When "Make It Run" Becomes a Security Incident
excerpt: How a university platform went from a successful prototype to a serious privacy and security failure—and how it should be rebuilt using secure design principles.
content:
## From Prototype to Production

The university platform in this case shows a problem in modern software development: a system can be technically functional while being fundamentally unsafe. Three students made a mobile-and-web platform in less than 72 hours with a lot of help from an AI coding assistant. The prototype worked enough to win a hackathon prize and organizations soon started using it for real tasks. The problem was that the developers treated a prototype as if it were ready for production.

The platform eventually held sensitive information, including student numbers, phone numbers, identification photos, GCash payment references, and private group messages. However, the security measures stayed at the level of a show. A user could change a profile number in a URL and see another student's information. Database passwords and an API key were put into a GitHub repository. Accounts had too much access to the database, error messages showed too much detail, and the system used plain HTTP.

These issues were not individual coding errors. They showed violations of Secure Design Principles. The important takeaway is that security has to be built into a system before it is responsible for protecting real people's information.

## Horizon One: The First Hours and Days

The first thing would be to stop the problem. I would take the application offline and put it into maintenance mode. Since the application is sharing information, leaving it online while checking it would make things worse. This goes back to the principle of safe defaults because access would default to being blocked rather than allowing people who should not have access to see records.

Next, I would replace every password and key that was found in the public GitHub repository. The exposed database password and payment API key should be thought of as broken even if there is no proof that someone used them. A secret that is out in the open cannot be trusted anymore. New passwords and keys should be kept in environment variables or a special secrets-management system instead of in the code. This follows least privilege and economy of mechanism by making sure only the right people and parts of the system can access important secrets.

I would also look into what information might have been seen. The team should check application logs, database access logs, GitHub history, and any other records to find out how much and how long the information was exposed. This is important because just removing the problem from the system does not tell us if someone already saw the data.

The broken profile authorization is very serious. The application used a profile identifier from the URL without checking if the logged-in user was allowed to see that record. This violates complete mediation, which means every time someone tries to see something, the system has to check if they are allowed. Just being logged in is not enough. The system must also check if the logged-in user is allowed to perform the action on that record.

For example, asking for /profile/1049 should not automatically give profile 1049. The server has to check the user's identity and permission before giving the record. Authorization checks must happen on the server and not rely on hidden parts of the interface or random URLs.

The database permissions should also be checked right away. Giving every account access to the database goes against least privilege. Users and parts of the system should only get the permissions they need for their job. If one account is compromised, it should not automatically give access to all the data of hundreds of students.

Finally, detailed error messages should be turned off in production. Error messages should be clear enough for people to know something is wrong without showing database queries, file paths, passwords, framework details, or anything else that could be used by someone trying to cause harm. This supports defense in depth because even if another problem exists, error handling does not give an attacker additional information.

## Horizon Two: Rebuilding the System Properly

After the urgent problem is fixed, I would rebuild the application with security being the focus, not just fixing the individual issues.

The first big change would be a proper system for authentication and authorization. Every sensitive request would go through server-side checks for permission. This brings back complete mediation. The application should use a deny-by-default model where access is given only when it is allowed.

I would also use least privilege throughout the system. Database accounts should have limited access. A part of the system that reads membership information should not also have permission to delete payment records. Admin functions should need permission, and users should only see the things that belong to their group or account.

The system should also use defense in depth. Security should not depend on one thing. HTTPS should protect the way clients and servers communicate. Authentication should protect accounts. Authorization should protect the things users want to see. Database access should keep damage low if the app is broken. Input checks should stop unexpected data. Logging and monitoring should help find unusual behavior. All these parts together give multiple layers of protection.

The principle of separation of privilege is also important. Sensitive actions should need extra permission and should not just be available to anyone who is logged in. For example, changing who owns an organization, seeing financial information, or handling admin accounts could require higher access.

The developers should also use open design. Security should not be based on hiding URLs or assuming attackers will not find the app's structure. The case relied on people not knowing the structure of the URLs. That is not a good way to be secure. A secure app should still be safe even if people know its parts and how it works.

The app should also follow psychological acceptability. Security should be easy for users to understand and use. If security steps are confusing, users might try to get around them. Good defaults, messages about who can see what, and simple account management features make it easier for users to be safe.

The way the team develops the app should change too. Before adding features, the team should think about what could go wrong. Code reviews should specifically look at authentication, authorization, secrets, input checks, error handling, and data leaks. Automated security tests should also be part of the development process.

## The Role of AI Coding Assistants

AI coding assistants can make building apps faster, but speed can give a false sense of safety: code that works is not always safe.

In this case, the AI-generated code made the app work. It probably made database access easier, but there were not enough checks for who could do what and there were unsafe ways to show errors. These are choices that might be acceptable for a quick test but are not okay for software that holds real student data.

The blame still lies with the developers. AI should be a helper, not a security expert. Developers must check the code that AI writes, understand what it does, test it, and make sure it follows security rules.

A good rule is that developers should not only ask, "Does this code work?" They should also ask, "Who can see this?", "What happens if this account is compromised?", "What information does this error share?", and "What happens if someone changes this ID?"

AI can make code, but it cannot take responsibility for what the code does.

## RA No. 10173 and Privacy Responsibilities

This situation is also linked to the Philippines Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The app was handling details like names, student numbers, phone numbers, photos, payment references, and private messages.

Developers working on apps that handle information cannot see security as just a technical thing. Their choices affect whether personal data is kept safe. They need rules, physical steps, and technical ways to protect personal data from people who should not see it, share it, change it, or do anything else with it.

This case shows why privacy should be considered when making a system, not after it is built. If developers know their app will hold documents and financial information, those risks should shape how the app is built from the start.

Privacy is not only the job of a privacy officer or someone in charge. Developers decide what data is collected, where it is kept, who can see it, how users log in, and what happens if something goes wrong. Those choices directly affect how safe people's data is.

## Speed vs. Responsibility

The students' biggest mistake was not using AI, working fast, or building a prototype. The real mistake was letting a test version become a real system without changing the way security was handled.

Fast building is useful in competitions and early tests. When a system starts holding real people's data, the standards have to change. The main goal becomes keeping the people who trust the system safe.

Principles like least privilege, complete mediation, safe defaults, defense in depth, separation of privilege, open design, economy of mechanism, and psychological acceptability help make that change.

AI tools help make apps faster. That makes secure development more important, not less. Developers must understand that code that looks good can still have security issues.

The goal is not to choose between making things fast or making them safe. The goal is to recognize when a project moves from being an experiment to something people depend on, and make sure that security, privacy, and responsibility grow with it. When an app has data from hundreds of students, "make it work" is no longer enough. The app must also be built so it deserves the trust those students placed in it.

title: Revisiting Our Risk Assessment Form Through the Eyes of an Auditor
content:
# Revisiting Our Risk Assessment Form Through the Eyes of an Auditor

## Introduction

When our group prepared the Risk Assessment Form for a small business, we focused on identifying possible risks, evaluating their impact, and recommending controls to reduce them. Our assessment covered common operational and information security concerns, including weak passwords, phishing, point-of-sale (POS) system failure, irregular data backups, internet outages, equipment theft, power interruptions, physical damage, outdated software, and former employees retaining account access.

However, looking at the same assessment through the eyes of an auditor changes the way we evaluate our work. Identifying risks is only the beginning. An auditor must also determine whether the organization knows what assets it owns, who is accountable for protecting those assets, and whether the controls described in its assessment are actually implemented and effective.

Our assessment provided a useful starting point, but it also highlighted an important lesson: **a recommended security control is not proof that the organization has implemented it or that it works.**

This reflection revisits our assessment from an auditor’s perspective while keeping the organization’s identity and internal information confidential. The discussion is based on our group's academic risk assessment, not a formal audit or verified on-site inspection.

## Understanding Which Assets Matter Most

The first question an auditor would ask is straightforward: What does the organization own, and which assets are essential to its operations?

In our assessment, the asset description repeatedly referred to daily business operations, sales, and information management. This helped connect the identified risks to the organization's activities, but it was too broad to serve as a complete asset inventory.

For example, a small retail or food-service business may depend on several important assets:

- **Point-of-sale systems and payment equipment:** These support transaction processing, sales recording, and daily business activities.
- **Business records and sales data:** These provide information needed for financial tracking, inventory decisions, reporting, and recovery after an incident.
- **Business accounts and credentials:** These control access to email, cloud storage, POS services, and other systems used by authorized personnel.
- **Computers, mobile devices, and network equipment:** These provide access to applications, business information, and internet-based services.
- **Software and cloud services:** These support daily operations and may store important business records.
- **Operational procedures and staff knowledge:** These allow employees to continue serving customers when technology becomes unavailable.

Not every asset has the same importance. Losing a temporary paper note may have a limited effect, while losing access to transaction records or a critical business account could interrupt operations and complicate recovery.

An auditor would therefore examine each asset's business purpose, the information it handles, its importance to daily operations, and the consequences of its loss, misuse, or unavailability.

The Center for Internet Security (CIS, n.d.) explains that organizations should maintain an accurate inventory of enterprise assets, including devices connected physically, remotely, virtually, and through cloud environments. Its guidance emphasizes identifying and managing assets so that organizations know what needs protection.

This supports one of our main observations: the risk assessment should be connected to a more detailed inventory. Without that inventory, the organization may overlook an asset, apply an unsuitable control, or struggle to identify which systems are affected by an incident.

## Classifying Assets and Assigning Ownership

After identifying important assets, the next step is to classify them according to their sensitivity and operational value.

A practical classification system could include four levels:

**Public.** Information approved for public distribution, such as general promotional materials and published business announcements.

**Internal.** Information intended for authorized business use, such as ordinary operating procedures and internal schedules.

**Confidential.** Information that could harm the business or individuals if disclosed without authorization, including nonpublic financial records and sensitive business information.

**Restricted.** Highly sensitive information requiring particularly strict access controls, such as administrative credentials, authentication secrets, and other information that could enable unauthorized access.

These categories are proposed examples rather than classifications confirmed during an actual inspection. The organization would need to define its own rules and apply them consistently.

Asset ownership is equally important. An auditor would expect each asset to have an accountable owner who understands its purpose, approves appropriate access, and ensures that risks are addressed. Technical maintenance can be delegated, but accountability should remain clear.

For example, a business owner or manager could be accountable for business records, financial processes, and critical accounts. A designated technical support person could maintain software updates, device security, and backup configurations. Employees could be responsible for following access procedures, protecting assigned equipment, and reporting suspicious activity.

The asset inventory should identify the responsible role, the department or operational area, the asset's location, its classification, and the date it was last reviewed. For digital assets, it could also record device identifiers, software versions, account ownership, backup arrangements, and relevant service providers.

CIS recommends documenting enterprise asset ownership and departmental responsibility as part of a detailed asset inventory (CIS, n.d.). This is important because an asset without a clearly assigned owner can easily be neglected. If a device is lost, an employee leaves, or a system stops working, the organization needs to know who is responsible for taking action.

Our assessment already assigned responsibility for proposed treatments to roles such as the owner, manager, or technical support personnel. That was a positive step. However, the next improvement would be to connect those roles to individual assets and document their accountability more precisely.

## What an Auditor Would Examine in Our Assessment

An auditor does not simply read a list of risks and accept every statement as accurate. The auditor seeks evidence that supports the organization's claims.

For our assessment, this would mean examining whether the existing controls described in the form are documented, consistently performed, and capable of reducing the identified risks.

The following areas would deserve particular attention.

### 1. Passwords and account access

Our assessment identified weak or shared passwords and the possibility that former employees could retain access to business accounts. Recommended treatments included unique passwords, a password manager, multifactor authentication (MFA), individual user accounts, and prompt account deactivation.

To evaluate these controls, an auditor could review account inventories, access policies, MFA configuration records, and documented employee onboarding and offboarding procedures. The auditor could also examine whether access permissions are periodically reviewed and whether departed employees' accounts are disabled promptly.

The objective would not be to collect or expose actual passwords. Instead, the auditor would verify the process and configuration without unnecessarily exposing confidential credentials.

### 2. Backups and recovery

The form identified irregular backups as a risk to business records. It recommended scheduled cloud backups and a separate periodic backup.

An auditor would request backup schedules, completion logs, failure notifications, retention policies, and records of restoration tests. A successful backup message alone is not enough to demonstrate that the organization can recover usable information.

A restoration test would provide stronger evidence that backed-up data can actually be recovered within an acceptable period. The organization should also determine which records are essential and how much data loss it can tolerate.

### 3. Software updates

Our assessment noted that updates were installed when notifications appeared and recommended a regular review of operating systems, POS software, and applications.

An auditor would examine software inventories, supported-version information, update records, and documented exceptions. These records would help establish whether all relevant systems are known and whether updates are being managed consistently rather than relying entirely on staff noticing notifications.

### 4. POS, internet, and power interruptions

The assessment proposed manual transaction records, fallback payment arrangements, an alternative mobile-data connection, and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) protection for important equipment.

To establish whether these treatments work, an auditor would review documented contingency procedures, equipment maintenance records, provider contact information, and evidence of operational tests.

For example, a written manual transaction procedure should explain how orders are recorded, how records are protected, and how transactions are reconciled when normal service returns. If the organization has never tested the procedure, its effectiveness remains uncertain.

### 5. Phishing and physical security

The form recommended basic phishing awareness training, verification of unusual requests, improved equipment placement, and secure storage of devices.

An auditor could examine training attendance records, awareness materials, incident reporting procedures, and relevant physical security policies. Where appropriate and authorized, the auditor might observe whether equipment is secured and whether access to important devices is limited to appropriate personnel.

The key principle across all these areas is consistent: **evidence should demonstrate what happened, when it happened, who was responsible, and whether the intended outcome was achieved.**

## Evidence That Would Make the Assessment More Reliable

A strong audit relies on more than interviews or written assurances. It combines different sources of evidence to build a reasonable picture of how controls operate.

For our assessment, useful evidence would include:

- An approved asset inventory showing identified assets, owners, classifications, and review dates.
- Account lists and access review records demonstrating that access is authorized.
- Configuration evidence showing that MFA and other applicable security settings are enabled.
- Backup logs and dated restoration-test results.
- Software inventories and records of completed security updates.
- Training records and documented procedures for reporting suspicious messages.
- Maintenance records and test results for backup power and other continuity arrangements.
- Incident reports, corrective-action records, and evidence that identified issues were resolved.
- Approval records showing who accepted any remaining risk.

An auditor would also check whether evidence is current and relevant to the specific control being evaluated. A policy written several years ago may not reflect current practices. A screenshot may show a setting at one moment without proving that it was maintained over time. An interview may explain a procedure without demonstrating that employees follow it consistently.

For that reason, evidence should be dated, traceable to the asset or control concerned, and retained securely. Sensitive screenshots, account details, and business records should be redacted or handled through authorized audit procedures when necessary.

The objective is not to collect the largest possible amount of documentation. It is to collect sufficient, reliable evidence to support a conclusion.

## Likely Gaps an Auditor Would Identify

Reviewing our form reveals several areas that deserve further verification and improvement.

The first is the lack of asset-level detail. The same broad asset description appears across multiple risks, making it difficult to identify which individual devices, applications, accounts, or records are affected. A separate inventory would make these relationships clearer.

The second is incomplete ownership information. Assigning a manager or owner to a treatment is useful, but the organization should also identify who is accountable for each asset, who performs the control, and who verifies that it is working. These responsibilities should not be assumed to be identical.

The third is the absence of supporting evidence in the assessment itself. The form describes existing controls, but it does not attach backup logs, account reviews, training records, maintenance reports, or test results. This does not prove that the controls are absent; it means their implementation and effectiveness cannot be established from the form alone.

The fourth is the need for stronger control testing. The effectiveness review assigns lower impact and probability ratings after the recommended treatments. These ratings express an expected reduction in risk, but they should not be treated as verified results unless the treatments have been implemented and tested. An auditor would ask what evidence supports each revised rating.

The fifth is the need for clearer follow-up. Treatments should have measurable completion criteria, target dates, supporting evidence, and a documented review. If an action is overdue or a control fails testing, the organization should record the issue, assign corrective action, and establish a new review date.

Finally, the assessment would benefit from a documented process for updating the inventory when equipment is purchased, software changes, staff leave, or services are replaced. A list that is accurate today can become unreliable when the organization changes.

These are potential documentation and assurance gaps identified from reviewing the academic form. Confirming whether they exist in actual operations would require interviews, observation, and evidence collection.

## Improving the Way We Evaluate Risk

One of the most important lessons from this review is that risk scoring and control assurance are related but different activities.

Our form uses impact and probability ratings to calculate an initial risk score and a residual score after proposed treatments. This is a practical method for prioritizing concerns. However, a lower residual score should reflect the control environment that actually exists, not simply the result expected from a planned action.

A more reliable process would record each treatment's implementation status, the evidence reviewed, the date of testing, the result, and any remaining limitations. If the control has not yet been implemented, the residual rating should be clearly marked as provisional or expected rather than confirmed.

The organization should also define what successful implementation means. For example, completing a backup configuration is one milestone; successfully restoring representative business records is a stronger test of recovery capability. Similarly, announcing an MFA policy is not equivalent to verifying that MFA is enabled for the relevant accounts.

This distinction would make our assessment more useful to management because it would show not only which risks matter, but also which treatments are complete, which controls require testing, and which risks still need attention.

## How an Asset Inventory and Audit Checklist Would Strengthen Our Recommendations

The next step is to turn our recommendations into a process that can be monitored and verified. Two practical tools would help: a detailed asset inventory and a repeatable audit checklist.

The asset inventory would identify what needs protection, who owns it, how important it is, and which controls apply. The audit checklist would help determine whether those controls have been implemented and whether they continue to work.

A basic checklist could include the following items:

| Audit item | Evidence to check |
|---|---|
| Asset inventory | Complete asset list, assigned owners, classifications, and review dates |
| Account security | Authorized account list, access reviews, MFA configuration |
| Backup and recovery | Backup logs, retention settings, successful restoration tests |
| Software maintenance | Software inventory, supported versions, update records |
| Business continuity | Written procedures, contact information, documented tests |
| Employee awareness | Training records and incident reporting procedures |
| Corrective actions | Assigned responsibilities, deadlines, completion evidence |

Each item should have a status such as *Implemented and tested*, *Implemented but not tested*, *In progress*, or *Not implemented*. The checklist should also identify the reviewer, date, evidence reference, and any corrective action required.

This approach is consistent with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, which provides guidance for identifying, prioritizing, communicating, and managing cybersecurity risks (Pascoe et al., 2024). Applying this framework would help the organization connect its risk assessment to ongoing management activities rather than treating the form as a document that is completed once and forgotten.

The inventory and checklist should be reviewed regularly and updated whenever meaningful changes occur. For a small organization, a simple spreadsheet and a manageable review schedule may be sufficient to begin. The important factor is not the complexity of the tools but the consistency with which they are maintained and used.

The process would also improve our group's risk treatments. Password improvements could be linked to access review evidence, backup recommendations could be linked to restoration tests, and software update recommendations could be linked to maintenance records. This would make it easier to determine whether a treatment reduced risk or whether additional action is necessary.

## Conclusion

Revisiting our Risk Assessment Form through the eyes of an auditor has shown us that identifying risks is only one part of effective risk management. An organization must also understand its assets, classify them according to their importance and sensitivity, assign clear ownership, and maintain reliable evidence that its controls are operating as intended.

Our group's assessment identified several relevant operational and information security risks and proposed practical treatments. However, the broad asset descriptions, limited asset-level ownership information, and absence of supporting control evidence in the form show why a more structured process would be valuable.

An auditor would not automatically conclude that a control is ineffective simply because its evidence is missing from the assessment. Instead, the auditor would seek further documentation, conduct appropriate tests, and distinguish confirmed weaknesses from matters that remain unverified.

Ultimately, an asset inventory and audit checklist would strengthen our recommendations by making responsibilities clearer, progress easier to track, and control effectiveness easier to demonstrate. They would also help management make better decisions about which risks require immediate attention and which improvements can be scheduled for later.

The most important lesson from this reflection is that **security is not established by writing down what an organization intends to do. It is strengthened by knowing what must be protected, assigning responsibility, implementing appropriate controls, and collecting evidence that those controls work.**

## References

Center for Internet Security. (n.d.). *CIS Critical Security Control 1: Inventory and control of enterprise assets*. https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-enterprise-assets

Pascoe, C., Quinn, S., & Scarfone, K. (2024). *The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0* (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 29). National Institute of Standards and Technology. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.CSWP.29
